title: Bridge shard orchestrator for KV cache across tensor/pipeline boundaries
creator: Ava Kim
description:
Background: On multi-GPU configs that mix tensor and pipeline parallelism we observe high memory fragmentation and suboptimal KV hit rates during continuous batching. Existing slab-based sharding assigns contiguous KV slabs per GPU which increases cross-stage prefetch traffic for long-context streaming workloads and forces frequent coarse-grained evictions under bursty prefix distributions.

Goal: Design and implement a lightweight orchestration layer ("Bridge Shard Orchestrator") that: 1) maps KV slices across tensor/pipeline boundaries to reduce cross-plane fetchs; 2) enables hot-key micro-replication for low-latency prefixes; 3) supports lazy cross-GPU prefetch and prioritized eviction that respects pipeline boundaries and runtime batch composition; and 4) integrates with continuous batching and the existing kernel scheduling heuristics.

Proposal summary: Introduce a bridge-shard abstraction: small, fixed-size KV shards (~8–64MB) that can be placed on one or more GPUs. A coordinator (per-pipeline) maintains a placement map and live metrics (access frequency, last-seen token index, pipeline stage affinity). Placement decisions are based on a cost model combining estimated cross-GPU transfer latency, local memory pressure, and predicted prefix reuse from continuous-batching statistics. Hot prefixes are proactively replicated on downstream stage GPUs (1–2 replicas) while colder shards remain single-placed. A lightweight lease protocol ensures only the coordinator mutates placement; workers use cached placement maps and fetch remotely when needed.

Key design decisions and trade-offs: 
- Granularity: use small fixed shards to balance placement flexibility and metadata overhead. This avoids per-key bookkeeping but is finer than previous slab sizes to reduce unnecessary transfers.
- Replication vs. Remote Fetch: replicate only very hot shards to bound memory overhead; use async remote fetch with prioritized prefetch for mid-hot shards to reduce tail latency.
- Coordinator locality: keep coordinator colocated with the first pipeline stage boundary in a pipeline replica to minimize control-plane RTT for placement updates.
- Eviction policy: eviction score = alpha * age + beta * remote-fetch-cost + gamma * hotness, where coefficients are tuned in experiments. This is a compromise between memory locality and transfer cost.
- Consistency: relaxed eventual consistency is acceptable for KV cache entries (they are cacheable, not authoritative). Lease windows are short (hundreds of ms) to allow adaptive re-layout during load shifts.

Implementation plan: 
1) Runtime shim: implement shard map data structures and RPCs for remote fetch/prefetch.
2) Coordinator service: placement engine that subscribes to continuous-batching telemetry (batch prefixes, sequence length histograms) and GPU memory metrics. Expose control flags (replication threshold, shard size).
3) Worker changes: fetch path fallback to remote fetch when local miss; prefetch path triggered by coordinator hints. Integrate with kernel scheduler so that prefetch windows align with token generation pacing.
4) Benchmarks & tests: unit tests for lease and placement updates; microbench for remote fetch latency; e2e streaming benchmarks (50 concurrent streams, variable prefix reuse) comparing baseline -> bridge shards.

Metrics to track: p50/p95 generation latency per token, remote-fetch rate, cross-GPU GB/s for KV traffic, eviction rate per-GPU, cache hit ratio by prefix-length buckets, memory headroom. Success criteria: p95 token latency reduced by >=10% under representative streaming workload and cross-GPU KV bandwidth reduced by >=20% vs baseline for those workloads, without >5% increase in steady-state memory used.

Rollout plan: behind feature flag at runtime-2.3. Staged rollout: internal canary on dedicated capacity (1 cluster) -> limited-hosted customers (opt-in) -> full default for new runtime pools. Include explicit fallback to previous slab sharding if eviction oscillation or p95 regressions are detected.

Risks and mitigations: 
- Oscillations under adversarial prefix shifts: add dampening and minimal placement intervals, and bounded move rate.
- Memory blowup from replication: enforce global replication budget and dynamic replica eviction when memory pressure rises.
- Increased control-plane overhead: batch placement updates and use delta maps for workers.

Dependencies: requires integration with continuous-batching telemetry ingestion (ENG-25681), and the kernel scheduler hooks for prefetch alignment (ENG-23890). Also depends on the NUMA-aware allocator improvements planned in ENG-48123 for accurate local memory pressure signals.
